title: Life for Life
theme: The Book of the Covenant begins by applying God's law to everyday life in Israel: the release of Hebrew servants, protection for vulnerable women, penalties for violence, and the principle of fair justice, life for life and eye for eye. A people freed from slavery must not become oppressors, and human life is precious.

language.note: 'These are the rules that you shall set before them.' Mishpatim are judicial decisions, usually case laws in the form 'If a man does X, then Y.' They show how the Ten Commandments work out in real disputes.

Often debt servitude rather than chattel slavery: a person who sold his labor to pay a debt. He was to go free in the seventh year without payment. The law begins with slaves because Israel had just been freed from slavery.

'Eye for (tachat) eye.' The word means 'in exchange for.' The principle (lex talionis) sets a limit: the penalty must match the injury, no more and no less, and it was applied by judges, not individuals.

A servant-wife who does not please her master must be allowed to be redeemed; he may not sell her to foreigners. The God who redeemed Israel requires that redemption shape how they treat the vulnerable.
Compensation is set 'as the judges determine.' The law places punishment in the hands of a court, not private revenge.

usage.note: Jesus quotes the principle and tells his followers not to use it as a personal right of revenge but to turn the other cheek. The principle remains the basis of just courts.
Deuteronomy adds that the freed servant must be sent away with generous provisions, 'remember that you were a slave in Egypt.' Jeremiah condemns Judah for breaking this law.
Because humans are made in God's image, murder must be punished, while cities of refuge protect those who kill by accident (v13).
A servant who loved his master could choose to stay for life, marked by an awl through his ear. Psalm 40, applied to Christ in Hebrews, speaks of ears opened and delight in doing God's will.

context.setting: After the Ten Commandments, God gives Moses 'the rules' (21:1-23:19), called 'the Book of the Covenant' in 24:7. They resemble other ancient law collections, such as the Code of Hammurabi, in form, but differ in important ways: they value human life above property, protect slaves and the poor, and rest on God's own authority and character.

flow.label: Hebrew servants
flow.note: A male servant goes free in the seventh year; he may choose to stay for life. A daughter sold as a servant-wife must be treated as family, redeemed, or set free.

flow.label: Capital crimes
flow.note: Murder, striking or cursing parents and kidnapping are punished by death. Accidental killing is distinguished from premeditated murder, with a place of refuge provided.

flow.label: Injuries
flow.note: Laws for injuries in fights, the beating of servants, harm to a pregnant woman, and the principle of life for life, eye for eye. A servant whose eye or tooth is knocked out goes free.

flow.label: Oxen and pits
flow.note: Responsibility for a goring ox and for an open pit. Owners who know of danger and do nothing are held accountable.

tier1.note: Jesus quotes 'eye for eye and tooth for tooth' and forbids personal retaliation.
Jesus quotes 'whoever reviles father or mother must surely die' to rebuke traditions that excused neglect of parents.
The servant law is restated with the command to give generously and the reason: you were slaves in Egypt.

tier2.note: Paul lists 'enslavers' (kidnappers, menstealers) among the lawless, applying this law against man-stealing.
The cities of refuge develop the provision for accidental killing.
Job will not despise his servants, for the same God made them in the womb.

tier3.note: Paul asks Philemon to receive Onesimus no longer as a slave but as a beloved brother.
In Christ there is neither slave nor free, a truth that undermines slavery from within.
God forms and knows the unborn child in the womb.

voices.name: Christopher J. H. Wright
voices.work: Old Testament Ethics for the People of God
voices.view: Wright argues that Israel's laws were a paradigm, a model of justice for a particular society that shows God's values. Compared with other ancient laws, they limit violence, protect the weak and value persons over property, and Christians should draw principles from them rather than copy them directly.

voices.name: Douglas K. Stuart
voices.view: Stuart stresses that Hebrew servitude was usually a form of debt repayment with built-in limits and protections, quite different from the race-based chattel slavery of later centuries. He sees the release laws as showing God's concern that no Israelite be permanently enslaved.

translations.kjv: If men strive, and hurt a woman with child, so that her fruit depart from her, and yet no mischief follow: he shall be surely punished, according as the woman's husband will lay upon him; and he shall pay as the judges determine.

renderings.text: so that her children come out, but there is no harm
she gives birth prematurely but there is no serious injury

translations.note: The Hebrew says her children 'come out.' Some read it as a miscarriage, with a fine for the lost child and 'life for life' only if the mother dies. Others, followed by ESV and NIV, read it as premature birth, so that 'harm' (v23) includes harm to the child, who is protected by the same 'life for life' rule.

translations.kjv: Then his master shall bring him unto the judges; he shall also bring him to the door, or unto the door post; and his master shall bore his ear through with an aul; and he shall serve him for ever.

renderings.text: his master shall bring him to God
his master must take him before the judges

translations.note: The Hebrew is ha-elohim, usually 'God.' It may mean before God at the sanctuary or before judges acting as God's representatives. Either way, the act was solemn and witnessed, not a private arrangement.

steps.gospel: A people redeemed from slavery must not enslave each other permanently, so the law limits servitude and requires release. These laws point to the God who frees, and finally to Christ, who 'took the form of a servant' and set captives free. The servant who loves his master and chooses to serve forever is a picture of the believer who, freed by Christ, gladly gives himself to him. And the principle of 'life for life' finds its deepest expression in the gospel: Christ gave his life in place of ours.
application: Treat employees, workers and the vulnerable with justice and dignity. God watches how the powerful treat the weak.
Value human life, from the unborn to the elderly. Murder and kidnapping were capital crimes because people bear God's image.
Do not take personal revenge. Justice belongs to proper authorities, measured and fair.
Take responsibility for dangers you know about. Negligence that harms others is a moral failure.
Remember that freedom in Christ is for loving service to him.

misapplications.claim: These laws prove the Bible approves of slavery as practiced in later history.
misapplications.correction: The law condemns kidnapping a person to sell him with death (v16), which was the foundation of the Atlantic slave trade. It limits Hebrew servitude to six years and frees servants who are injured (v26-27). Its direction is toward protection and release.
It was a rule for judges (v22) to keep punishment proportionate. Jesus forbids using it for personal retaliation (Matthew 5:38-42).

contrasts.note: The law weighs intent, providing refuge for the accidental killer but not for the murderer, even at God's altar.
Servants have legal protection; abuse leads to their freedom.
The penalty must fit the harm, a check on cycles of violence.

features.label: Casuistic law
features.note: Most laws use 'If... then' cases rather than broad commands. They teach principles through examples judges could apply to other situations.

features.label: Beginning with slaves
features.note: The first case concerns servants, deliberately recalling Israel's own slavery. God's people must remember where they came from.

features.label: Ancient Near East parallels
features.note: Laws about goring oxen also appear in the Code of Hammurabi, but Exodus treats human life as worth more than property and protects servants more strongly.

steps.summary: Exodus 21 turns the Ten Commandments into case law for daily life. It limits servitude, protects women and servants, distinguishes murder from accidental killing, and sets proportionate justice as the rule for courts. Behind it is a redeemed people who must not become oppressors and a God who values every human life.

metaArc.book: Chapter 21 begins the Book of the Covenant (21:1-23:33), which applies the Ten Commandments and is ratified in chapter 24. It shows that worship of the LORD shapes justice in society.
metaArc.redemptive: This belongs to Redemption: the redeemed are to live justly and mercifully. It points to Christ, who frees from slavery and gives his life as the ultimate 'life for life.'
